summary: Workflow-sized tasks can remove repeated outer-pipeline mechanics and preserve shared context, but the supplied evidence supports them only as a conditional exception to dependency-linked cards, not as a general token-saving rule.

points.text: Agent Studio's measured corpus places 98.1% of recorded tokens in coding runs and about 1.9% in four review aspects. Avoiding repeated reviews has a bounded visible token benefit; avoiding coding setup, retries and duplicated context is what can change the result materially.

The same corpus reports 4,949 minutes, or 16.6% of compute, in deterministic test gates while their model-token count is zero. Gate repetition matters for latency and throughput, but it is not evidence that collapsing cards saves model spend.

A workflow is strongest when at least three slices are independent, bounded and path-disjoint, and one end-to-end gate can validate the combined delivery. Sequential API, schema or migration decisions are durable card boundaries, not workflow fan-out opportunities.

No controlled Agent Studio experiment has run the same task both ways. The break-even formulas are a decision model and must be updated with per-agent tokens, attempts, diff size and review findings from the first workflow cohort.
